passage: Two days before the municipal election in Pandharpur, a pamphlet appeared under every door. "If the other party wins, your temple land will be taken!" Big red letters, no names, no source. Farida, twenty, a political science student, read it at the tea stall. Around her, uncles were already angry. She felt her own stomach tighten, then noticed how the words were built to scare. She asked, "Who printed this?" Nobody knew. That evening she and her friend Trisha went to both parties' ward meetings. They asked each candidate about the temple land. Neither had any plan to take it. Farida wrote a short, calm message for the neighbourhood group: what each party actually promised, with their own words. A few people replied "thank you." One uncle called her naive.

qa.q: Where did Farida read the pamphlet?
qa.a: At the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when her stomach tightened?
qa.a: She felt a flash of fear and alarm, the same the pamphlet wanted, before she noticed the scare tactic.

qa.q: What did Farida do well in handling the pamphlet?
qa.a: She asked who printed it, heard both sides directly and shared what each party actually said, calmly.

qa.q: How might the uncle who called her naive see things?
qa.a: He may feel she is too trusting of politicians, or be unwilling to let go of his fear.

grounding: A small-town student questions a fear-based election pamphlet and checks both parties' actual positions.

passage: In a Berlin café, Selin, twenty-one, spread two newspapers on the table: one she always read, one she never did. Her friend Mateo raised an eyebrow. "Punishment?" "Experiment. Same story, migration policy." She read hers first and nodded along. Then the other one. Her jaw tightened; the columnist's view annoyed her. But she made herself underline claims, not feelings. Then she did the same with her own paper. That was harder. It had phrases like "heartless officials" and "a flood of hatred." Emotional words, doing the thinking for her. "Both sides have a point on one thing," she said slowly. "And both are selling me a feeling." Mateo grinned. "Welcome to adulthood." She wrote a note: check sources, not only headlines.

qa.q: What was the story about in both papers?
qa.a: Migration policy.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when her jaw tightened?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and resistant, disagreeing with the columnist's view.

qa.q: What approach helped Selin evaluate both views fairly?
qa.a: Underlining claims rather than feelings, and applying the same test to her own paper.

qa.q: How does Mateo react to Selin's conclusion?
qa.a: Mateo seems amused and approving, joking that she has grown up.

grounding: A young woman in Berlin compares opposing papers and notices emotional manipulation in her own side too.

passage: Madhav Sir leaned back in his office chair. "Zubin, you asked how to handle your first freelance contract. When I was twenty-two, a small firm offered me a logo project. The deadline was one week. The fee was half what I'd hoped. I wanted to just say yes; I was scared they'd walk away. But I thought about what I needed and what they needed. They needed it fast. I needed fair pay and time to do it well. So I said: 'Ten days instead of seven, and half the fee in advance.' They paused. Then they said, 'Nine days, and forty percent upfront.' I said yes. It wasn't everything, but it was fair for both. That firm gave me work for four years." Zubin tapped his pen. "What if they'd said no?" "Then I'd have known what they valued."

qa.q: How long was the original deadline?
qa.a: One week.

qa.q: How did young Madhav feel when he first got the offer?
qa.a: He felt tempted to say yes immediately, scared the firm would walk away.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Madhav's negotiation?
qa.a: Thinking about what both sides needed and proposing a specific trade: more time and part of the fee upfront.

qa.q: How might the firm have seen young Madhav's counter-offer?
qa.a: They likely saw him as professional and reasonable, which is why they met him partway and kept working with him.

grounding: A senior colleague tells an intern how he negotiated a fair compromise on his first freelance contract.

passage: The landlord, Siddharth Rao, needed an answer by six, and it was already five. Sumit, twenty-one, stood in the empty flat in Hyderabad with his phone at ten percent. The rent was fine, but the geyser didn't work and the window latch was broken. "Take it or leave it," Siddharth said. "Three others are interested." Sumit's heart raced. He wanted the flat; it was near his college. He took a breath. "I'd like to take it. Could you fix the geyser before I move in? I'll fix the latch myself, and I can pay the first month today." Siddharth frowned, glanced at the geyser, then nodded. "Geyser by Monday. Deal." Sumit shook his hand, relieved and a little amazed at himself.

qa.q: By what time did Siddharth Rao need an answer?
qa.a: By six.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when his heart raced?
qa.a: He felt anxious and pressured, wanting the flat but worried about losing it.

qa.q: What made Sumit's offer work under pressure?
qa.a: He stayed calm, asked for one key fix, offered to handle the smaller one and showed he was ready to commit.

qa.q: How might Siddharth Rao have seen Sumit's proposal?
qa.a: He likely saw it as reasonable and reliable, a quick way to secure a tenant.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young man negotiates a key repair with a landlord by offering something in return.

passage: Chandrika, twenty-two, had a new job at a Pune marketing firm and an evening design class she'd paid for before she was hired. The class started at five on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Office ended at six. She rehearsed the conversation in the washroom mirror. Then she knocked on her manager Chetan's door. "I'd like to ask for something, and offer something." He looked up. "Go on." "Could I leave at four-thirty on Tuesdays and Thursdays? I'll start at eight those days, and I can cover the Saturday client calls nobody likes." Chetan tapped his pen. "Saturday calls every week?" "Every other week." A pause. "Deal, for three months. Then we review." Chandrika walked out, hands shaking, and let out a quiet breath.

qa.q: What time did Chandrika's class start?
qa.a: At five.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling as she walked out with shaking hands?
qa.a: She felt relieved and a little shaky, after being nervous about asking.

qa.q: What made Chandrika's request persuasive?
qa.a: She asked clearly, offered something valuable in return, and agreed to a compromise with a review date.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Chandrika after the conversation?
qa.a: He likely sees her as proactive and fair, willing to give something back for what she asked.

grounding: A young employee negotiates flexible hours with her manager by offering a mutually beneficial trade.

passage: I'm Ankita. Two years ago, my brother Sachin dropped me at the railway station for my first term at college in Delhi. I had one big suitcase and a steel dabba of Amma's laddoos. I remember feeling like I might float away with excitement. My own room! No curfew! Then the train started, and Sachin was waving, and I suddenly wanted to jump off and go home. I sat there crying and grinning at the same time, and the aunty across the seat offered me a tissue without a word. That first month, I called home every night and also stayed out till ten every night. Both were true. I didn't know you could want to leave and want to stay so badly at the same moment.

qa.q: What did Amma pack for Ankita?
qa.a: A steel dabba of laddoos.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel as the train started?
qa.a: Ankita felt excited and scared at once, crying and grinning, wanting both to leave and to go home.

qa.q: What could help someone going through the same mixed feelings on leaving home?
qa.a: Letting both feelings be true, keeping regular calls home while also exploring the new freedom.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt waving at the station?
qa.a: Sachin may have felt proud and a little sad to see Ankita go.

grounding: A young adult looks back on the mix of excitement and fear on leaving home for college.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, first-year boys' block. Pradeep Iyer. Week 3.
Varun, Room 22, seems to be enjoying his freedom: late nights, cricket in the corridor, food runs at midnight. But on Sunday I found him on the terrace at ten, on a call with his mother, voice thick. Afterwards he told me, "Sir, I love it here. I also want to go home. Is that weird?" I told him it was normal and that most first-years feel both. He laughed, a bit embarrassed. I suggested he pick one evening a week to call home properly, and also join the photography club he'd mentioned. I will check in with him next Sunday.

qa.q: Which room is Varun in?
qa.a: Room 22.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling on the terrace?
qa.a: He felt torn: happy with his freedom but also homesick, missing his mother.

qa.q: What did Pradeep Iyer suggest?
qa.a: A regular evening to call home and joining the photography club.

qa.q: How might Varun's mother feel during the call?
qa.a: She may have sensed he was homesick and felt both worried and glad he called.

grounding: A warden's note records a first-year student holding both excitement about freedom and homesickness.

passage:
Tuesday night. Elizabeth's journal.
The email came at 4:12 p.m. I got it. The job in Bengaluru. Actual salary, actual desk, actual city far away from everything I know. I screamed in the library and got shushed. Then I went outside and sat on the steps and felt like I might throw up. I don't know anyone in Bengaluru. What if I'm bad at it? What if I'm lonely? Tushar called and said, "You're allowed to be scared and happy." That helped a bit. I made two lists: things I'm excited about (my own flat, the work, the weather) and things I'm scared of. The scared list is longer. But I'm still going. I'm writing the acceptance email tomorrow morning.

qa.q: At what time did the email come?
qa.a: At 4:12 p.m.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel after getting the job?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt thrilled and terrified at once, excited about the job but scared of being lonely or failing.

qa.q: What helped Elizabeth deal with the mixed feelings?
qa.a: Tushar's words, and making two lists to see both the excitement and the fear clearly.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel about Elizabeth's news?
qa.a: Tushar likely feels happy for Elizabeth and wants to be supportive.

grounding: A young adult's journal captures the conflicting joy and fear of accepting a job in a new city.

passage:
College counsellor's note. Yogesh Nair. Thursday.
Akash, second-year engineering, came in saying he couldn't focus. As we talked, it came out that he'd been thinking a lot about summers at his grandmother's house in Kottayam: jackfruit, cousins, falling asleep on the verandah. He said, "Everything was simple. Nobody asked what my plan was." He smiled while saying it, then looked close to tears. I told him that missing a simpler time is a common feeling when life gets heavier, and that it can sit alongside moving forward. I suggested he call a cousin from those summers, and write down one thing from that time he could bring into his week. We'll meet again in two weeks.

qa.q: Where was his grandmother's house?
qa.a: In Kottayam.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he smiled and then looked close to tears?
qa.a: He felt bittersweet, warm memories mixed with sadness and longing for a simpler time.

qa.q: What did Yogesh Nair suggest Akash do?
qa.a: Call a cousin from those summers and bring one thing from that time into his week.

qa.q: How might a cousin feel getting a call from Akash about those summers?
qa.a: The cousin might feel touched and nostalgic too, glad to share the memories.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a student longing for the simplicity of childhood summers.

passage:
Saturday. Deepika's diary.
Clearing out my room before the move. Found the shoebox under the bed. My school ID with the terrible fringe. A friendship band from Class 6. A comic Omkar and I drew together, with a superhero cat. I sat on the floor for an hour. Back then, the worst problem was Omkar hiding the TV remote. Now it's rent and deadlines and people who don't reply to emails. I laughed at the cat and then cried a bit. I miss being small. I also don't want to go back. I took a photo of the comic and sent it to Omkar. He replied, "Captain Meow lives!" I packed the box to take with me.

qa.q: What was the superhero in the comic?
qa.a: A cat.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel looking at the old comic?
qa.a: Deepika felt bittersweet, laughing and crying, missing the simplicity of childhood while not wanting to go back.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel receiving the photo?
qa.a: Omkar seems delighted and nostalgic too, replying playfully.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows bittersweet longing for childhood while packing to move.

The bus pulled out past the fields and the temple, and he pressed his forehead to the window, heart racing, not with fear but with something bigger. "Here we go," he whispered.

passage: In their tiny Toronto dorm kitchen, Jin and Emeka had a map of the city stuck to the fridge. Graduation was five weeks away, and they'd signed the lease for their first real apartment, above a bakery. "We'll be able to smell bread every morning," Jin said, circling it with a marker. Emeka was already listing furniture from a free-stuff website. "A sofa. A real one. Not a beanbag." "And a big table for dinners," Jin said. "Your jollof, my dumplings, every Friday." They both laughed. Emeka paused, looking at the circled square. "It feels like the start of something." Jin nodded, grinning so hard his cheeks hurt. "Five weeks," he said.

passage: Alka Bua sat with Naveen on the steps. "You're drowning with your first job, na? When I was twenty-one, your grandfather had his stroke. Overnight I had to handle everything: the hospital bills, the bank, my new job, your Dadi's medicines, the house. One evening I sat on the hospital bench with a pile of forms and couldn't move. I just stared. A nurse, Sister Mary, sat next to me. 'One form,' she said. 'Just the top one.' I filled it. Then the next. Then I called my cousin and asked her to handle the bank. It took me weeks to feel like a person again. But I learned: when everything comes at once, you don't carry it all at once." Naveen let out a long breath.

qa.q: Who sat next to young Alka on the hospital bench?
qa.a: Sister Mary, a nurse.

qa.q: How did young Alka feel on the hospital bench with the pile of forms?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and paralysed, unable to move.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Alka's story?
qa.a: Sister Mary telling her to do just the top form, and then young Alka asking her cousin for help with the bank.

qa.q: How might Sister Mary have seen young Alka that evening?
qa.a: She likely saw a frightened young woman frozen by too much, and wanted to help her take one small step.

grounding: An aunt tells Naveen how, at twenty-one, she was flooded by sudden adult responsibilities and began coping one step at a time.

passage: It was Monday, 9 p.m., and Jahnavi, twenty-two, had three weeks at her first job, rent due tomorrow, and her mother's insurance forms that had to reach the hospital by noon. Then her phone died. She sat on her floor in the Kolkata flat, laptop open, cursor blinking, and couldn't type a single word. Her friend Ojas knocked with a charger. He found her staring at the wall. "Talk." "It's everything," she said. "I don't even know where to start." He sat down, took a paper, and wrote three lines: rent, forms, sleep. "Rent first. Five minutes." She did it. "Forms: call the hospital helpdesk at nine tomorrow and ask what's missing." She nodded, breathing easier. "Sleep. Now." She laughed shakily. "Okay."

qa.q: By what time did the insurance forms have to reach the hospital?
qa.a: By noon.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she couldn't type a single word?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and frozen, flooded by too many responsibilities at once.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that helped?
qa.a: He broke everything into three small steps, starting with the quickest, and suggested asking the hospital helpdesk.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt finding Jahnavi staring at the wall?
qa.a: He was probably worried about her and wanted to help calmly.

grounding: A young woman is overwhelmed by work, rent and a parent's insurance forms, and a friend helps her break it down.

passage: Arohi, twenty-one, had been in Gurugram for two weeks. On her laptop were seven open tabs: rent agreement, tax declaration form from HR, health insurance choices, an electricity connection request, her bank's new account page. She sat staring at them for an hour on Sunday, not clicking anything. Her chest felt tight. Her flatmate Amandeep came in with chai. "You've been frozen like that since lunch." "I don't know what any of this means. Mumma always did this." Amandeep sat beside her. "Close everything except one." Arohi closed six tabs. "Rent agreement. Read it with me. The tax one, we'll ask HR on Monday." Arohi breathed out. "I thought adults just knew." Amandeep laughed. "Nobody knows. We ask."

qa.q: How many tabs were open on Arohi's laptop?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling as she stared at the tabs for an hour?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and anxious, paralysed by unfamiliar adult tasks.

qa.q: What approach helped Arohi get unstuck?
qa.a: Closing all but one tab, reading the rent agreement together and saving the tax question for HR.

qa.q: How does Amandeep see Arohi's struggle?
qa.a: Amandeep sees it as normal, reassuring her that nobody just knows and everyone asks.

grounding: A young woman in her first job freezes before a flood of adult paperwork until her flatmate helps her take one task at a time.

passage:
"Lakshmi, you haven't touched your tea."
"I'm fine, Irfan."

"I know."

Irfan slid the tea closer. "Drink. I'm not going anywhere tonight."
She held the cup with both hands. "Thank you."

qa.a: Five years.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She felt deep sorrow and grief, not just for the person but for the whole future she had planned.

qa.q: What did Irfan do that helped Lakshmi?
qa.a: Irfan listened quietly, said she was allowed to grieve, and stayed with her.

qa.q: What is it like for Irfan to sit with Lakshmi's grief?

passage: I'm Indu. For three years, I tried to get into medical college. Three attempts at the entrance exam. The third time, I missed the cut-off by eleven marks. I didn't cry that day. I'm in a biotechnology course now. Some days I like it. Some days I still miss the doctor I was going to be.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when seeing the old white coat?

qa.q: How might Anand have felt watching Indu's disappointment?
qa.a: He likely felt sad and protective, sharing in the grief.

passage: Afreen Nani pulled her dupatta closer. "Rajni, you keep fighting what's already happened. Let me tell you about when I was twenty. I'd won a scholarship to study in Hyderabad. Two weeks before I was to leave, my father's shop burned down. There was no money, and my mother needed me at home. I raged for a month. I wrote letters to the college, cried every night, blamed everyone. Then one morning, sorting burnt stock in the ash, I thought: this is what is. I can keep fighting it, or I can decide what to do next. I stayed. I taught at the local school. It wasn't the life I planned. But it became a good one." Rajni looked at her hands. "Did you ever stop missing it?" "No. But I stopped fighting it."

qa.q: What happened to young Afreen's father's shop?
qa.a: It burned down.

qa.q: How did young Afreen feel during the month after the fire?
qa.a: She felt angry and grief-stricken, raging and crying every night.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Afreen's story?
qa.a: Sorting burnt stock in the ash and deciding to accept what was and choose what to do next.

qa.q: How might young Afreen's mother have felt when Afreen decided to stay?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and grateful, though perhaps sad for her daughter's lost chance.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at twenty, she learned to accept losing a scholarship after a family crisis.

passage: The email came the day before Yusuf's internship was to begin: the Chennai start-up had shut down. He read it on the bus in the pouring rain, his phone screen blurry with drops. For a moment he wanted to call them, argue, demand something. Then he laughed, a short, stunned laugh. There was no one to argue with. He called his mentor, Kavitha Ma'am. "I had my whole summer planned." "I know. What's still true?" He thought. "I still have the skills. And three free months." "So what do you want to do with them?" By the time he got off the bus, soaked, he had a list: two small companies to write to, one online course, and a week at home to rest. It wasn't his plan, but it was a plan.

qa.q: Where was the start-up that shut down?
qa.a: In Chennai.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he laughed a short, stunned laugh?
qa.a: He felt shocked and frustrated, then a kind of resigned acceptance that there was no one to argue with.

qa.q: What did Kavitha Ma'am's question help Yusuf do?

qa.a: She likely feels proud that he adjusted quickly and calmly.

passage: Mehak's parents had decided to sell the Andheri flat where she'd grown up. They were moving to a smaller place in Thane; the building was being redeveloped and the offer was fair. Mehak, twenty-two, first argued. Then she stopped, because there was nothing to argue about. On the last Sunday, her friend Rashmi helped her pack her old room. Mehak ran her hand along the wall where her height was marked in pencil, 1998 to 2012. "I'm not going to fight it," she said quietly. "It's just... sad." Rashmi took a photo of the pencil marks. "For you." Mehak smiled, eyes wet. She packed the last box, closed the door, and didn't look back more than twice.

qa.q: Where were Mehak's parents moving?

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling as she ran her hand along the wall?

grounding: A young woman accepts that her childhood home is being sold, letting herself feel sad without fighting it.

passage:

July: His mentor, Vasudha Ma'am, called. "You were two marks short. Two. Come and see me." He went. They sat with his answer sheet and marked every mistake. He made a new timetable, with mock tests every Sunday.
Next May: Santosh sat the prelims again, hands steady this time. In the evening, he wrote in his notebook: "Whatever happens, I did it properly." He slept well for the first time in weeks.

passage: Siddharth Uncle cleaned his glasses. "Harish, you think one failure means you're done? At twenty-two, I started a small tiffin service with two friends. We cooked in my mother's kitchen, delivered on cycles. Within eight months, we'd lost everything we'd put in. One friend left. I cried in that kitchen, I won't lie. For a month I didn't want to see a tiffin box. Then my mother said, 'Did you learn nothing?' I had learned a lot: we'd priced too low, and delivered too far. So I tried again, alone, only offices within three kilometres. It was hard, and slow. That's the company I run now." Harish looked at his own laptop, where the rejected application was open. "So I just try again?" "You learn, and then you try again."

qa.q: How did they deliver the tiffins?
qa.a: On cycles.

qa.q: How did young Siddharth feel after the business failed?
qa.a: He felt crushed and discouraged, crying and not wanting to see a tiffin box for a month.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Siddharth's story?

qa.q: How might the friend who left have seen young Siddharth's second attempt?
qa.a: That friend might feel surprised and perhaps a little regretful, seeing Siddharth succeed.

grounding: An uncle tells Harish how he recovered from a failed business at twenty-two and tried again.

passage: Uma, twenty-one, had sent out twenty internship applications and received twenty rejections. On the day the twenty-first came back no, her laptop screen cracked. She sat in the Kolkata college library on a borrowed computer, tired and furious. Her friend Arnab found her there. "Take a break?" "No." She pulled up a spreadsheet. "I'm finding out what's going wrong." They went through every application. Her cover letters were identical; she'd never named the company's actual work. "Okay," she said, jaw set. "New letters. Each one different." She wrote three that evening, until the library closed. Arnab walked her to the bus stop. "You're kind of scary right now." Uma laughed for the first time that week. "Good."

qa.q: How many rejections had Uma received before the twenty-first?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she set her jaw?
qa.a: She felt frustrated but determined to fix what was going wrong.

qa.q: What change did Uma make after studying her rejections?

qa.q: How does Arnab see Uma's determination?
qa.a: Arnab is impressed and a little in awe, joking that she's scary.

grounding: Despite many rejections and a broken laptop, a young woman studies her mistakes and tries again.

passage: Gautam Mama put the carrom board on the table. "Trisha, you work till midnight every day. When I was twenty-two and started at the bank, I did the same. After six months, I couldn't sleep, and I snapped at everyone. One Sunday my roommate dragged out this board. 'One game,' he said. I laughed so hard at his terrible shots, I nearly fell off my chair. I forgot the bank for two hours. After that, every Sunday, carrom, no matter what. My work didn't get worse. It got better, because I was a person again, not just a desk." Trisha raised an eyebrow. "And you still play?" "Forty years. Now, strike first, or are you scared?"

passage: It was exam week, and it was raining hard in Mangaluru. Omkar, twenty, had been at his desk for nine hours. His eyes ached. His roommate Joseph appeared in the doorway with a football. "Twenty minutes." "Are you mad? It's pouring." "Exactly. Nobody else will be on the field." Omkar groaned, then followed. They slid, splashed and missed every shot, laughing like children. Joseph fell flat in a puddle. Omkar laughed so hard he couldn't breathe. When they came back, soaked and muddy, Omkar's head felt clear for the first time in days. He opened his notes and understood a page that had confused him all afternoon. "Same time tomorrow?" Joseph asked. "Only if it rains."

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling after they came back soaked?
qa.a: He felt refreshed and lighter, his head clear for the first time in days.

qa.a: It relieved his stress, so he could understand a page that had confused him all afternoon.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt when Omkar laughed at his fall?
qa.a: Joseph likely felt happy and amused, glad his plan worked.

grounding: During exam week, a student takes a playful break in the rain and returns to studying refreshed.

passage: Every Friday night in their Bengaluru flat, Chetan and Gautam held the "Worst Chef Challenge." Rules: three random ingredients, fifteen minutes, one judge: the neighbour's cat, who always walked away. This Friday it was bread, bananas and pickle. Chetan, twenty-two, had had a terrible week: a deadline missed, a manager's cold email. He wasn't in the mood. Gautam put an apron on him anyway. By minute ten, Chetan was frying banana-pickle sandwiches and laughing at the smell. Gautam's creation looked like a small brick. The cat sniffed both and left. "Draw," Gautam declared. Chetan collapsed on the sofa, still laughing. He hadn't laughed like that all week. "Same time next Friday," he said.

qa.q: What were this Friday's three ingredients?
qa.a: Bread, bananas and pickle.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel before the challenge started?
qa.a: He felt stressed and low after a terrible week, not in the mood.

grounding: Two young flatmates keep a silly weekly cooking game going as a counterweight to work stress.
